The heart arrives without a calendar. That is the strange thing Aaron notices later, when he tries to lay the pieces end to end and finds there is no end and no beginning he can trust—only a set of rooms he has stood in, none of them dated, none of them owing the others anything he can prove.

There is a kitchen table with a clinic form on it, and Della's hand flat on the wood, asking him to sign while there is still time, because what is in the freezer is all there will ever be of him. There is a cardiology clinic, sometime, a doctor with numbers, weeks not months, a muscle that is finished. He cannot say which came first, the asking or the diagnosis, only that both live in him at once, side by side, like two rooms with the same window.

There is a boy's baseball field, Wes with scripture inked into both forearms, testifying to nine-year-olds about a mercy he has only just discovered, while Nita watches from the bleachers the way you watch weather. There is a road crossing. There is a pickup that does not stop, then stops, then does not stop again. There is a hospital corridor where a woman is told about her husband, and then, while she is still holding the first sentence, about both her children, and her whole life is removed from her in the time it takes to say it twice.

There is an operating theatre Aaron only knows from the inside of sleep—waking able to breathe for the first time in what feels like years, lying still to listen to a heart that is not the one he was born with. There is a police station, a man walking up the steps on his own, waiting at the counter, telling a sergeant what happened at the crossing and how far he drove before he came back. There is a house with the girls' drawings still taped to the wall, and a woman in the bathroom with the door locked, starting again the way you start a job.

There is a car park where Aaron pays a stranger to break every rule there is, and is handed a name and a street. There is a swimming pool where he arranges to be in the water at the same hour, day after day, until it stops being a coincidence and becomes an affair. There is a kitchen where he says it badly—whose heart, whose chest—and is thrown out that same night, and asked back four days later, and goes.

There is Della again, or still, hearing that he does not want the child after all, and saying the true thing: that he is spending a life somebody else paid for. There is a prison gate, a family waiting on the far side of it, and a man who looks at them and keeps walking, four hundred miles, to a motel with rooms that need cleaning.

There is a house where a woman says she cannot breathe in the same country as the man who did it, until that is the only sentence left in the rooms. There is a lock-up, a pistol changing hands. There is a wall behind a motel in the dark, a shot that goes somewhere it will not kill, a voice telling a bleeding man to get up and run.

There is a doorway, later or earlier, Wes standing in it asking to be finished, and the gun turning the wrong way in Aaron's hand.

There is a car with the horn down, a hospital, a heart that has already changed hands once refusing to go on beating for a stranger a second time. There is a man walking back toward a family he left at a gate. There is a woman going home alone, carrying something that has no name yet.

None of it will stack into a line. Aaron has tried, lying in bed with his hand on his own sternum, to make the accident come before the transplant, the transplant before the pool, the pool before the gun—but every order he builds collapses back into a single room with too many doors, all of them open at once, all of them the same hour.

Tobias wakes with a headache and a strange flatness. There is nobody in his head who was not there two years ago. He lies still, trying to name the missing weight, and cannot.

Inside his own head, hours earlier, he had stood in the worst of it — the shouting, the door, the dent in the car — and watched each room lose its walls while he was still in it. The ugly part went first. He let it go without much grief.

He gets to the platform for work and, for no reason he can give anyone, gets on the other train instead. He rides to the end of the line and walks out onto frozen sand, and a woman with dyed hair is already standing on it, as though she had been waiting for a stranger she didn't know she was expecting.

When the machine reached the memories he wanted to keep, he had started to run, carrying her into rooms she'd never been in — a childhood kitchen, under a table, anywhere the map did not go. He could not explain, even to himself inside his own skull, why he had changed his mind.

They drive back into the city talking too easily for strangers. Outside her building she asks him up for a drink as though it were the second time.

Two technicians had let themselves into his flat at night. One of them, called Peck, quietly slid the bagged mementos — a hairslide, a mug, a torn page — into his own coat, and stood there a moment holding everything that had once made a woman love somebody.

They sit in her stairwell, months later, two envelopes open on the step, listening to their own recorded voices give the reasons it ended, and she runs, and comes back up, and they decide to do it anyway, knowing exactly how it goes.

Before that, on the last night in his flat, the two on the outside — Dell and a receptionist named Rosa — had been drinking his beer and dancing on his bed in their underwear when the map on the screen stopped corresponding to anything, and neither of them noticed for a long time.

He goes to the bookshop to make it up with her, once, in the old life, before any of this, and she looks at him the way you look at a customer. A young man is behind the counter with her, laughing at everything he says. Tobias does not yet know his name is Peck.

Dr. Hallam had been called out at three in the morning to put the erasure back on its rails. In the hallway Rosa kissed him, and his wife, arriving behind him, told her exactly why she had always felt that way about him and could not remember why.

He takes the form letter Nina and Grady hand him straight to Hallam's office and asks to be given the same thing he's just watched done to him — the same nothing — that afternoon if possible.

The last thing left in his head, that last night, was the shore house on the night they met. In the doorway of a room already going, she told him to walk out, and then to come and find her at the coast.

He fills two carrier bags with everything that has her in it, so the machine can find the memories they're pinned to.

Two years earlier they had lain out on the ice of the frozen river, steamed the windows of a noodle house, sat in the back seat at a drive-in with the sound turned low, and he had been happy in a way he could not describe to anyone.

She takes herself to a shabby clinic and pays to have a man removed from her head, every room, every argument, every good afternoon, as though he had never been in it.

And at the very start, at the end of the rail line, on a cold beach full of strangers, a man with nothing to say to anyone had ended up talking to a woman with dyed hair. They broke a window of a shuttered house on the shore and slept on the boards, and neither of them could have said, afterward, what it was that made them begin.

Rosa quits the clinic not long after, and empties the filing cabinets on her way out, and posts every patient their own file — forms, object lists, tapes — so that everyone erased might finally be handed the evidence of what they'd lost, and what, without knowing it, they had already chosen again.

Mr. Ash carried him in with his boots dragging blood down the ramp and laid him on the concrete like something that might still be salvaged. "Nobody dies here today," he said, holding the man's head off the ground, and the man he called Elm screamed and believed him for exactly as long as it took to stop believing anything.

It had gone wrong inside a minute. The alarm was already running when they came out, and Ash had put his arm through the window and fired both ways at once while the car went down a street none of them recognized. On foot after that, Elm had dragged a woman out of her own car and she'd had a gun in the door pocket and put one into his stomach before he could get the door shut. He'd shot her. He hadn't meant to remember her face, and now he would, if there was time left to remember anything.

He had not always been called Elm. Months before, in a bare room with a folding table, a handler named Pruitt had walked him through a story about a bag of drugs and four dogs in a public lavatory, again and again, until he stopped reciting it and started remembering it as if it had happened to him. He had told it to Bram and Cal and Ash in a bar with the laugh landing exactly where Pruitt promised, and walked out with a job and a name he hadn't picked.

Now that name was bleeding out on a warehouse floor, and Birch arrived clean and furious, saying the police had been on the pavement before the first alarm, that somebody in this room had made a call, and then he went out and hid the stones where no one watching him could see.

Ren came in late, unhurried, complaining about the noise, and opened the boot of his own car to drag out a young officer in uniform, wrists bound. Nobody asked why he had one. Nobody, that day, was owed an explanation the way Ren was owed his freedom — he'd done his stretch without opening his mouth, and Bram had paid him back in trust and a place on the job.

Left alone with the officer, Ren found an oldies station, danced a few steps to it, took the man's ear off with a razor, and poured petrol over him without raising his voice.

Elm shot him from the floor. Every round he had left went into the man holding the lighter, and then, because Doyle deserved that much, he told him what he was — a police officer — and that there were cars outside waiting on Bram.

Cal came back to find the body and the story and decided the story held. Then he put three rounds into Doyle himself, to close the matter, and the only witness who could have confirmed anything was gone.

Bram walked in and looked a long time at the man on the floor. "This is the one," he said, flat as a fact, and Ash put his gun on Bram instead and would not be told otherwise — the man had carried him, had promised him he wouldn't die, and would not now be talked out of that promise.

Three guns came up in a room the size of a garage and all three went off. When it stopped, Bram and Cal were done making any noise at all, and only Ash and Elm were still breathing, badly.

Elm told him then, because the man had earned it and because there was no more use for anything but the truth. Ash dragged himself upright, put the barrel to his own skull, and the doors came in as he fired, and they cut him down where he knelt — the last man in the room who had believed the anecdote was a memory, and the promise a fact, right up until both turned out to be exactly what they were.

He said one word and let the glass globe go, and it rolled off the boards and broke on the step, and that was how Emmett Rusk died, alone in a palace he had never finished building.

The newsreel ran nine minutes in a screening room full of men who had never met him. It showed the palace, the papers, the two wives, the politics, the collapse, and it explained nothing at all. Nash sat at the back and wrote the word down on his cuff because he had no paper handy. Bluebell. He was told to find out what it meant.

He started with the wrong woman first, or the right one, depending. Nora was drunk at a table in a seaside club at four in the afternoon, and she told him to get out before he had finished asking. So he went looking backward instead, into the record, because that was the only direction the dead allowed.

He read Barrow's memoir in a marble library and learned how it had started — a mining town, a lodger who couldn't pay board leaving a worthless deed that turned out not to be worthless at all, a mother signing her son over to an eastern banker with the money still warm on the table. The boy had gone down into the yard with a sled and put it into Barrow's stomach hard enough to sit him down, and had been taken east that evening anyway, as though the sled had never happened. On his twenty-fifth birthday, with the whole estate finally his, he had told Barrow that out of all of it he wanted the loss-making newspaper, because he thought it might be fun.

Marsh remembered the rest better than anyone living. The bed moved into the Clarion offices. The statement of principles signed and printed over his own name. The whole staff of the rival paper bought outright and danced into a party with a brass band, Emmett dancing in the middle of it. Then the trip abroad for statuary, and the engagement to the governor's niece that put the wedding on every front page but his own.

Nash didn't need anyone to tell him how that one ended; he'd seen enough breakfast rooms in his life. Devlin filled it in anyway — the talk shortening, the table lengthening, until husband and wife sat at opposite ends reading rival papers, one of which he owned.

Then the shopgirl with toothache, laughing at the mud on his coat, and the secret rooms, and Halloran bringing the wife up the stairs ten days before the ballot to offer a trade Emmett wouldn't take. The paper he owned had printed FRAUD AT THE POLLS across six columns rather than let anyone think he'd been made to bend. Devlin had asked for a transfer that week. The marriage had gone without either of them raising a voice.

Then Nora, bought a singing teacher and a house to sing in, made to be seen as something she wasn't. Devlin, brought back for the debut, had gotten drunk instead of writing kindly and fallen asleep mid-sentence, and Emmett himself had finished it, printed it, and fired him for it. Nora had swallowed poison rather than go out in front of them again, and only then had he let her stop.

He'd shut her away in Silvermount after that, in ceilings too high to heat, crates never unpacked, jigsaw puzzles laid out on a floor the size of a station. A picnic on a black beach that nobody enjoyed. A quarrel. She had packed in the morning and gone, and he had torn her room apart afterward and stopped at a glass globe full of snow, and said the word to nobody, and carried it past mirrors that gave him back smaller and smaller until he disappeared.

Nash put his notebook away in the marble hall, telling Marsh and Devlin and Nora and old Colm the butler that no single word ever explains a life. Below them, workmen were clearing the crates out at last, and a small sled marked BLUEBELL went into the furnace with the rest, and nobody in the house saw it go.

THEN

Elias Prine sat across the desk with his hands folded, telling Martin Kray the same story twice without noticing. Martin wrote *psychosomatic* on the form and denied the claim. No injury, no payout, nothing further to discuss.

NOW

Martin came out of a motel bathroom he did not remember entering and found a telephone already lifted to his ear. He kept talking. He was telling a story about a man named Prine who could not hold a memory longer than a few minutes. He did not know why he kept telling it, only that the man on the other end always let him finish.

THEN

Elias's wife moved the clock forward and asked, sweetly, for her injection. He gave it to her. She waited a while and asked again. By the third time she was on the floor and by the fourth he was calling for an ambulance he could not later recall calling.

NOW

The caller gave him a name — Gil Marsh, a dealer, an address — and Martin wrote it in block letters on a card already crowded with other cards.

THEN

Two men came through the bathroom door. Martin shot one across his wife's body. The other put his skull into the mirror, and after that nothing new would stay.

NOW

In a basement with standing water Martin beat the dealer until his hands hurt and finished it with a belt. He took a photograph. The dying man said one word — *Elias* — that meant nothing, and Martin, not knowing why, put on the dead man's suit and drove off in his car.

THEN

Martin built himself out of paper: photographs pinned in rows, notes clipped to notes, and along his ribs and thigh the handful of facts he had decided he could trust forever.

NOW

A plainclothes man named Roy found Martin at the derelict building where Gil's photograph still curled from the heat of a lighter. Roy said the dealer had been nobody. Said the real man had died a year ago, with Roy standing beside him while he pulled the trigger. Said the story about Prine was not a story. Martin burned the photographs instead of believing him, wrote *he is lying to you* across Roy's face, and copied his license plate off the car at the curb as the next true thing.

THEN

A year earlier, in that same building, Roy had walked Martin to a stranger and stood by while Martin shot him. Within minutes Martin was asking who they'd come to find.

NOW

Martin sat in a tattoo parlor with a note crushed in his fist and had the plate driven into his thigh below five other facts, not remembering the hand that wrote the note.

THEN

Out in a field, long before any of this, Martin burned a hairbrush and a stack of paperbacks that had belonged to his wife, trying to grieve something that would not stay burned in him.

NOW

Behind her own bar, a woman named Corinne watched a stranger walk in wearing her boyfriend's suit and park his car outside. She smiled, took his order, and let the staff spit in the beer before it reached him.

THEN

Martin, newly amnesiac, filled his rented room with a system meant to survive him — photographs, captions, ink under his own skin — because his handwriting was the only witness he could still call reliable.

NOW

Corinne cleared every pen from her house first. Then she said the words that made him swing, waited outside for the bruises to rise, and came back blaming a man named Vance.

THEN

Elias's claim, six months gone, sat closed in a drawer while his wife's death was filed as accidental. Nobody connected the two men who would later share nothing but a basement and a whispered name.

NOW

Martin waited in a motel bathroom's dark, took Vance down as he came through the door, and drove him to the edge of town at gunpoint with a warning he would forget delivering.

Corinne ran the plate through a friend at the registry and set the printout in front of him: Roy Mercer, in full.

Martin lured Roy back to the derelict building on a pretext, walked him into the room, and put one through his head. He photographed what was left, satisfied, at last, that the note in his pocket had been right all along.

He did not know why he kept telling it, only that the man on the other end always let him finish.

THEN

Elias's wife moved the clock forward and asked, sweetly, for her injection. He gave it to her. She waited a while and asked again. By the third time she was on the floor and by the fourth he was calling for an ambulance he could not later recall calling.

NOW

The caller gave him a name — Gil Marsh, a dealer, an address — and Martin wrote it in block letters on a card already crowded with other cards.

THEN

Two men came through the bathroom door. Martin shot one across his wife's body. The other put his skull into the mirror, and after that nothing new would stay.

NOW

In a basement with standing water Martin beat the dealer until his hands hurt and finished it with a belt. He took a photograph. The dying man said one word — *Elias* — that meant nothing, and Martin, not knowing why, put on the dead man's suit and drove off in his car.

THEN

Martin built himself out of paper: photographs pinned in rows, notes clipped to notes, and along his ribs and thigh the handful of facts he had decided he could trust forever.

NOW

A plainclothes man named Roy found Martin at the derelict building where Gil's photograph still curled from the heat of a lighter. Roy said the dealer had been nobody. A year earlier, in that same building, Roy had walked Martin to a stranger and stood by while Martin shot him. Within minutes Martin was asking who they'd come to find.

NOW

Martin sat in a tattoo parlor with a note crushed in his fist and had the plate driven into his thigh below five other facts, not remembering the hand that wrote the note.

THEN

Out in a field, long before any of this, Martin burned a hairbrush and a stack of paperbacks that had belonged to his wife, trying to grieve something that would not stay burned in him.

NOW

Behind her own bar, a woman named Corinne watched a stranger walk in wearing her boyfriend's suit and park his car outside. She smiled, took his order, and let the staff spit in the beer before it reached him.

THEN

Martin, newly amnesiac, filled his rented room with a system meant to survive him — photographs, captions, ink under his own skin — because his handwriting was the only witness he could still call reliable.

NOW

Corinne cleared every pen from her house first. Then she said the words that made him swing, waited outside for the bruises to rise, and came back blaming a man named Vance.

Elias's claim, six months gone, sat closed in a drawer while his wife's death was filed as accidental. Nobody connected the two men who would later share nothing but a basement and a whispered name.

Martin waited in a motel bathroom's dark, took Vance down as he came through the door, and drove him to the edge of town at gunpoint with a warning he would forget delivering.

The gold watch came to Denny before anything else did. A man just off a troop ship sat him down in a bare front room and put it in his hands, told him his father had kept it hidden through years in a camp so that one day it could be exactly this: a small boy's, ticking. Denny wore it after that the way other men wore a name.

Everything else in this story is business.

Rollo and Marcus crossed the city arguing about what foreign countries called a hamburger and whether their drug laws made any sense, guns zipped in a bag on the back seat, saying nothing about the job because there was nothing to say about it yet. In the corridor outside the flat they kept arguing, this time about a foot massage, whether it was worth a man getting thrown off a balcony for touching another man's wife that way. Then the door, and the scripture Marcus recited to a young man named Tobin before they shot him for skimming money from Otis, and the briefcase they took off the floor by his body. A fourth man came out of the bathroom and emptied a revolver at them from six feet and hit nothing, and Marcus stood in the spray of holes behind him and called it a miracle out loud, the first time in his life he'd meant a religious word.

In the car after, his gun went off over some remark and took the head off Del in the back seat, and that ended the morning's talking. Marcus drove the ruined car to Warren's garage, where a soft fixer hosed them down in borrowed shorts and T-shirts and had the whole thing gone in under an hour, like it had never happened.

They stopped for eggs on the way to deliver the case. Two strangers at the next booth decided over coffee that nobody ever robs a restaurant, and were up with a pistol before the plates were cleared, and Marcus — carrying that morning's miracle around in him like a coal — handed over his own wallet and talked the boy down and let the two of them walk. He kept the briefcase. He and Rollo brought it to Otis's bar in their borrowed clothes, and found Otis at the counter paying a boxer named Denny to go down in the fifth.

Rollo drove out that same stretch of days to buy from his dealer Kip, pure stuff, shot up at the kitchen table, and that night took Otis's wife Nadia to a dance contest at a diner dressed up like an old movie, and they won it barefoot. Back at the flat she found the bag in his coat, thought it was something else, and nearly died on Kip's carpet before a needle of adrenaline brought her back.

Denny did not go down in the fifth. He killed the other man instead and was in a taxi before the crowd understood it. He and Marielle ran for a motel, where she told him she'd left the watch on the bedside table. He went back for it anyway, into a flat that was already occupied — Rollo, waiting with a submachine gun laid on the counter closer to Denny's hand than to his own, which was the whole of the mistake. Denny walked out with the watch back on his wrist and one more body behind him.

Driving off he found Otis crossing the street with a paper bag in his arms and put the car through him. Both wrecks were dragged into a pawnshop basement by men who owned the place, and Denny got free once, stood at the door with the street open in front of him, and went back down anyway, took a sword off the wall, and settled it. Otis told him afterward they were square, so long as he was gone by morning.

He collected Marielle from the motel, put her on a motorcycle lifted from the shop, and rode out past the last lit windows of the city with the watch ticking against his wrist, the only thing he'd carried all the way through that was worth carrying.

I. THE DOG

Four adults, a baby and a dog in a house built for two. Ruben slept on the couch and watched his brother's wife move about the kitchen and told himself it was nothing, and his mother kept the peace by not asking questions. The dog, Tigre, came back one night off the street having killed something bigger than itself, and a neighbour explained what a thing like that was worth. Within a month Ruben was walking him into a pit twice a week, and twice a week he was walking him out again, and the money went into a hole in the wardrobe that Ruben thought nobody else knew about.

It went well until the night the promoter had lost too much on one fight and put a pistol into the dog's side in the middle of the ring. Ruben went over the rope with a knife before he had decided to, and then he and Pipo were in a truck going through a red light at sixty with the dog bleeding across the back seat, and the truck took the side out of a small car turning across the junction.

A vagrant pushing a cart of scrap stood in the smoke afterward, looked at the wreckage and the people running toward it, and lifted the bleeding animal out of the back seat and carried it away before anyone thought to stop him. His name was Cardo. He fed the dog by hand in a yard full of strays until it slept against him and followed him into the street each morning. Then one evening he came home to find every other dog in the yard dead and Tigre standing among them with its muzzle wet, and he held a gun to its head a long time and could not fire it.

II. THE HOUSE

Nestor robbed a chemist's with a scarf over his face and came home and knocked his wife across the kitchen for asking where the money had gone, and Ruben started saying, quietly and then not quietly, that she should come away with him. He paid two men in a bar to break his brother's bones for it. Nestor worked out who had arranged it in about a day, and left with Alma, the baby, and every note Ruben had hidden in the wardrobe.

Years seemed to pass in that one week. Nestor went into a bank with the same scarf and was shot on the floor of it. At the funeral Ruben made the offer one last time, and Alma looked at him and said no, and meant it, and he understood that she had never once been going to come.

III. THE FLAT

Hector left a wife and two daughters at a birthday party and moved Celine into a flat with a floor-to-ceiling window facing her own billboard. She was in the small car at that junction when the truck came through the light. She woke in the hospital with a cage of pins holding her leg together and asked first about her lapdog Chispa, left alone in the new flat and now nowhere to be found. It had gone through a gap in the boards and could not get back, and its whining came up through the floor of every room while Hector tore the boards up one by one and her leg went bad above him. The leg came off above the knee. That same week the billboard across the road was stripped and pasted over with something else, and the two of them sat in the wrecked flat looking at the blank frame.

IV. THE MAN WHO DIED

Elian met Cardo behind a church and paid him to kill his own half-brother, Sergio, and Cardo took him instead to a yard and chained him to a bed frame among empty kennels. He had stood a long way back at his wife's funeral among people who believed him dead twenty years, and had followed his grown daughter Perla home through three streets. He brought Elian face to face with Sergio, set a loaded pistol between them, and walked out with money from both. Then, shaved, in clothes that did not fit, he let himself into Perla's flat, spoke his whole life onto her answering machine, took one photograph from her shelf, left his money on her table, and walked with the dog out into the flat grey wasteland at the edge of the city.

I hadn't slept in six months when I found out that grief buys sleep as well as anything, even grief that isn't yours. Four evenings a week I sat in folding chairs in church halls, holding hands with dying strangers, weeping for diseases I did not have, and it worked. I was an insomniac product-recall investigator with a system.

Then Ada Vey started showing up, smoking through the meditation, and the moment I could see the lie in her I could see it in myself. The sleep stopped.

On a night flight not long after, I sat next to a soap salesman named Rex Marrow who talked for forty minutes about how everything I owned had been chosen for somebody else. I kept his card because it seemed like the sort of thing you keep.

I want to tell you now, out of order, what it comes to: a stairwell, service lights buzzing, my own hand around a gun I thought belonged to someone across from me, the muzzle in my mouth, the angle wrong until I fixed it, and the understanding, arriving about half a second too late to matter, that the man taking me down those stairs one flight at a time was never anyone but me. I pulled the trigger and shot through my own cheek to kill him. That happens later. I'm telling you now so that when it happens again, at its proper place, you'll know what you're looking at.

Back before that: my flat went up in an explosion, the catalogue furniture with it, and I called the number on the card instead of calling her. Rex took me into a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district with no working plumbing and better opinions than any house I'd owned.

Outside a bar he asked me to hit him as hard as I could. We beat each other bloody in the car park and I felt, for the first time in longer than the insomnia, something that was entirely mine. It became a weekly thing in a cellar. Then a waiting list. Then rules read aloud at the start of every session.

Ada overdosed and called, and Rex brought her back to the house, and the two of them were audible through every floor while I lay rigid downstairs, unable to stand what I couldn't yet name.

Rex rendered stolen fat from a cosmetic clinic into soap on the kitchen stove and sold it back to the department stores at eighty dollars a bar. He burned my hand with lye and held it down when I tried to leave into meditation, into the cave, into anywhere but the minute. I still have the mark. I blackmailed my employer with my own beaten face and got paid to stay away.

The cellar became an organization. Rex called it Havoc. Shaved men filled the house, slept on the floor, went out to break things belonging to companies. Then Rex drove us into oncoming traffic, let the car roll, and was gone when I came to in the ditch, and was gone everywhere after that.

Ogden was shot dead coming out of a job with a drill in his hand, and I started trying to stop what I'd made. I went city to city and found the same cellar under every bar, the same rules on the same wall, and men who looked up and called me Rex.

In a motel room, with flight records and receipts across the bed, it went together: one body, one bank account, one man awake and one man asleep, every conversation with him held in an empty room. I called Ada and asked whose bed she'd been in. Mine, obviously, she said, and what's wrong with you.

I found the vans under the debt-record towers, wired and timed, and understood at last what the whole thing had been built toward. I went in to defuse them, and Rex — I still call him that, it's easier — beat me down the stairwell, and at the bottom I did what I told you already: put the gun in my mouth and fired through my own cheek to kill him.

They brought Ada up afterward, delivered by shaven men who apologized and left. We stood at the window, my face wrapped, holding hands, and watched the towers come down in order, one after another, exactly as planned.

Above the noise, at an open window, an old man was telling a younger one that nothing survives time. He said it without bitterness, as a fact of chemistry, the way you'd say water finds its own level. Below them the street was still full of blue light, and neither of them looked down at it yet.

They were carried out through the crowd with their hands behind them, Cort shouting, Jonah silent, into that same light. One arm hung wrong at Cort's side. Neither man looked back at the club they'd been dragged from.

Inside, a few feet from the extinguisher and the body under it, the man they had actually been hunting stood watching with everyone else, unremarked, unbothered, a stranger among strangers. Jonah had gone on swinging long after the man on the floor stopped moving.

It hadn't taken long to get there. In the club Cort had pulled faces out of the dark until he chose one, and the one he chose had taken his arm at the elbow and turned it until something in it came apart. Before that, two men had detached themselves from a doorway and offered, for money, a name and a place to drink it. They pointed down the street toward the basement steps.

Before that, outside a party, Cort and Jonah had come into the night air still half-laughing and stopped, because there was a trolley on the pavement and a blanket and a face on it they both knew.

Before that, in the tiled dark of an underpass, a man had had a woman by the hair and was beating her without hurry against the concrete, and a passer-by at the far end had looked, hesitated, and walked on. She had gone into the underpass instead of crossing four lanes of headlights, not thinking twice about it, the kind of decision that isn't a decision at all until afterward.

She had left the party alone before that — Cort three drinks past being any fun, working the room, and she'd watched him a while, said nothing, collected her coat. On the train down they had all three been arguing cheerfully, the argument of people who expect to argue again tomorrow, about sex and about how much he'd already had.

That morning had begun in complete safety: a park, sprinklers turning over the grass, children running through the spray, and she lay on her side with a book she wasn't reading, one hand flat on her stomach. Before that, alone in the flat, she had sat on the edge of the bath with the stick in both hands and let herself smile at it before telling anyone. And before that, in bed with Cort in the thin morning light, she had described a dream — a red tunnel she kept walking into — while they traded lazy insults about the man she used to live with, who was now only a friend, and the three of them had been easy and close in a way that made none of it seem like a beginning of anything.

Now the old man at the window was still talking, gesturing loosely down at the street as if it illustrated his point better than words could. Nothing survives, he said. Not buildings, not marriages, not the shape of an afternoon. The younger man across from him said nothing.

He did not know, could not have known, watching the light spin off the police car roofs, that the girl on the trolley hours before had been carrying something that would never be spoken of again, or that the man responsible was standing free in a basement a hundred yards off, having watched two strangers destroy themselves in his place. The old man only knew the shape of the argument, not its evidence. But evidence was gathering all the same, in ambulances and holding cells and a park that no longer existed except as a fact someone had once been foolish enough to trust.

Below, they put Cort and Jonah into the car and closed the doors, and the street went on holding its light a while longer before it, too, let it go.

Nadir stood at the gun-shop counter with Sahar beside him, translating for a man who did not need translating so much as patience, and the dealer behind the glass repeated his vowels back at him in a voice pitched for the security camera's amusement. Nadir paid and left with the pistol in a paper bag and something worse than fear settled into his chest.

Nadir would kneel in the street afterward and decide the child was an angel sent to spare him. But that was still ahead of him on the night he walked out of the gun shop with Sahar's hand on his arm.

Within the week Paula would stand at the top of her stairs while a locksmith named Mateo fitted new locks, telling her husband, loud enough for Mateo to hear, that the tattooed one would be selling their keys to his friends by morning. Mateo said nothing and went to fit the lock on a shopkeeper's door next — Nadir's door, twice broken into already — and warned him that the lock was never the real problem, the door itself needed replacing. Nadir heard a man inventing a second job for himself and threw him out.

Officer Boyle pulled over a couple named Renee and Clay for nothing at all, and searched Renee with his hand somewhere it had no business being while Clay stood three feet off and said nothing. His partner Voss went to their commander the next morning and said he couldn't ride with the man anymore, and got a new car for the price of a lie about flatulence, and thought that settled something.

It did not. Boyle sat across a desk from a clerk named Delia Frank, begging for his father's treatment, and was refused, and lost his temper at her badge. And it was this same Boyle who, not long after, crawled into an overturned wreck with petrol pooling toward a fire and dragged Renee out by the arms — the same hands.

Nadir's shop, exactly as Mateo had warned, came apart in the night. The insurer read the file and declined, citing the warning he'd refused. He stood in the wreckage of his own stock with nothing coming to him, and that was the night he loaded the pistol and went to wait outside Mateo's house.

Trey and Kwame ran down a small man named Pham between parked vans and left him breathing outside a hospital, arguing the whole way there about what they'd just done — not knowing yet that his van, found later, would be packed with trafficked people whom Trey, alone, would drive to the docks and set loose, giving them what was in his pockets.

A man was dragged from his own stolen car at gunpoint by four officers who'd been told wrong, and it was Voss again who walked into the middle of it and talked them down — the man was Clay. Clay drove the boy who'd once carjacked him, Trey, out of the city at speed and put him out on the verge without a word, which was how Trey came, eventually, to be standing at the docks with strangers walking free into the dark.

Voss picked up a hitchhiker in the rain, misread a hand going into a pocket, and shot him twice. The body in the ditch turned out to be Kwame, and the detective called to find him was his own brother, Reece, who recognized the shoes before he recognized the face. His mother told him, on her kitchen floor, that she'd asked him a hundred times to go and look and he never had.

Paula fell down her own stairs with no one home and told her housekeeper, in the ambulance, that Alba was the only friend she had.

Snow came for the first time that winter. Two cars touched at a junction, and the shouting started before anyone looked at the damage.

All night the helicopters went over, low and steady, spraying the fruit fly and everybody's washing, the same drone at the same hour over every roof in the city, and nobody who heard it thought it had anything to do with anyone else.

Under one of those roofs, Neil Hartigan buttoned his shirt for the second time while his wife Bess, a painter, worked in her studio full of unfinished bodies until the last possible minute, neither of them looking forward to the dinner they had agreed to give.

At a bakery across town, a woman named Elaine chose a design from a book and wrote a name and an age on a card. Otto the baker said Monday, and please collect it promptly. The name was Charlie Rill.

On his way to school not long after, Charlie stepped off a kerb and a waitress named Rhona, hurrying, caught him with the wing of her car. He got up, said he was fine, refused a lift, and walked the rest of the way home insisting on it.

That night he went to sleep on the sofa and did not wake up properly. After that there was a room with a machine in it, and his parents, Grant and Elaine, taking shifts in a chair. Into that corridor came Grant's father Duff, a man nobody had seen in years, who could not think what to say into the silence and so told his son about a woman from decades back, an affair, delivered like comfort and landing like nothing else could have.

Because no one came to pay for the cake or collect it, Otto, unpaid and ignored, began ringing the Rill house at two in the morning to say the boy's name, again and again, until it became the cruellest habit in his day.

Elsewhere, Cheryl folded nappies with the phone against her ear, walking men through fantasies from her living room while her husband Stu sat three feet away going quietly incandescent. Days later Stu drove out with Vern and two others to fish, and found a young woman face down in the shallows. They tethered her ankle to the bank so she wouldn't drift and fished on for two more days before telling anyone. When Vern told it at his own kitchen table, his wife Iris, still half made-up as a clown from a birthday job, stopped with the sponge in her hand, disgusted at what he'd been willing to stand beside.

Across the city Vida sang six nights a week to a room mostly talking through her, while at home her daughter Bee practiced cello alone into an empty house.

Officer Rowe needed a reason for having been out and so drove the family dog to the far side of the valley and left it, telling his wife Peg it must have jumped the fence — a lie built to cover an affair with a woman named Nan. When Nan's ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot, learned she had a new man, he spent an afternoon sawing every chair and table she owned into pieces.

House-sitting for the Hartigans, Ike and Dot made each other up as a beaten corpse and photographed it in the hall, laughing.

At the dinner party itself, over the fish, Bess told Neil about the modelling session years ago, and then the thing after it, and Neil set his glass down very carefully and made the whole table watch him fall apart.

The machine was switched off the next morning. Charlie died. That afternoon Grant and Elaine drove to the bakery to shout at Otto about the calls, and he sat them down instead and fed them warm bread and grieved with them, the only reconciliation in the whole business, and it was between strangers.

Bee came home from rehearsal, found her mother asleep in the chair as always, and went out to the garage and pulled the door down.

At a picnic in the hills, Stu, still carrying whatever the river had left in him, picked up a rock when a girl said the wrong ordinary thing.

Then the ground moved for eleven seconds, and by the evening bulletin every death, every wrecked chair, every drowned girl and every quiet lie in the city had been folded into the same three minutes of news.

Solly Two Coats had never worn robes before, and he thought they suited him. He and his crew walked into the diamond house like men who'd renounced the world, and walked out with the one stone worth renouncing it for.

Marv called from overseas before the dust settled. Bring it straight over, he said, in the voice of a man who did not enjoy repeating himself.

Grigor the Nail had a talent for arranging collisions. He told Solly about a good bookmaker's, a place worth a wager, and in the same breath told Ike and Benno, two pawnbrokers with more nerve than sense, that the same shop was ripe for robbing.

Meanwhile Halloway and Digby sent their fighter Pretty Sam to buy a caravan off the travellers, a job that should have taken an hour. It ended with Sam on the ground and a bare-knuckle man named Finn standing over him, having settled the negotiation with his fists. Halloway now had no fighter for Coldstone's rigged bout, and no choice but to put Finn in instead. He promised Coldstone that Finn would go down in the fourth.

Solly landed in the city, delivered his stone to the fence Hersch for safekeeping, and carried an empty-seeming case to the bookmaker's to place his bet. Ike, Benno, and a third man, Tulley, bungled the job entirely — they seized Solly's arm and his case in the chaos, then fled straight into Grigor, who chased them off, furious that his tidy arrangement had gone sideways.

In the ring, Finn ignored every instruction and knocked his man cold in the first round. Coldstone lost a fortune and turned his anger on Halloway.

Marv, arriving to find neither cousin nor diamond, hired a bounty hunter named Ledge, a man who found treasure by following its clumsiest handlers.

Grigor, believing the case held the stone, took Solly apart to open it — cut off his arm for the lock — and found nothing inside. The diamond had never been there at all.

Ledge tracked the pawnbrokers down, shot their car apart, and took both men and the recovered stone into his custody.

Coldstone fed what remained of Solly to his pigs, and told Halloway and Digby exactly what would happen to them if the second fight went wrong.

Halloway and Digby relayed the order to Finn — down in the fourth — and Coldstone's men, to make the point permanent, burned Finn's mother alive in her caravan.

Grigor, still hunting the stone, ambushed Ledge's car with the pawnbrokers inside. In the gunfire that followed, Ledge, Grigor, and Benno all died, and the diamond was left loose on the street.

Tulley, the last man standing from the botched robbery, got away with nothing but a stray dog — the same dog that had swallowed the diamond in the confusion.

The travellers, grieving and armed, waited for the rematch. Finn held his instructions exactly — down in the fourth — and then broke them, knocking his opponent out cold on schedule while the travellers moved through the crowd and slaughtered Coldstone's men.

Halloway and Digby found Coldstone alone in the wreckage of his own plan and shot him. By morning the travellers had vanished from the city entirely, taking their dead and their silence with them.

The dog, still carrying its swallowed prize, was handed in at a pet shop days later, and coughed the diamond up in front of a startled clerk. It was Halloway and Digby, of all people, who ended up holding it — two men who had never robbed anyone, standing at the end of every theft and every death with the stone that had cost so many lives finally, absurdly, in their hands.

Emlyn arrived at Wilder's house the same evening the telephone call had shaken loose something between them, and he sat down as though he had been expecting the summons for years rather than hours. He told Wilder, without any of the heat Wilder had braced for, that he had known for four years. Odile had told him on the trip abroad, in the hotel where a letter in Wilder's hand had been waiting at the desk. He said he had never thought much of his friend's letters either, and that this, more than the affair itself, seemed to amuse him. Wilder sat very still, understanding at last that every lunch, every dinner, every civil evening of the last four years had been conducted by a man who already knew everything and had chosen to say nothing.

That knowledge cast back over the whole shape of what had come before. Two years earlier, in a bar, Odile had told Wilder that her marriage was over, that she had spent the previous night confessing everything to Emlyn — the affair, the rooms, the child she had once carried and called her husband's. She had believed, telling it, that she was delivering news. She had let slip, almost carelessly, that Emlyn had for some time been publishing a writer Wilder represented, a writer both men quietly despised, and it was that detail, more than the confession, which had sent Wilder to the telephone in a state, demanding to see his friend.

Before that bar, before the unravelling, there had been the closing of the rooms — Wilder and Odile deciding, without any discovery to force them, that the crockery should be split and the lease surrendered, that the affair had become a chore rather than a household. Before that, the long charade of dinners: Emlyn and Wilder at the married couple's table discussing racquets and schoolboy sport while Odile sat with no part in the talk at all, excluded from a friendship she could not enter. Before that, the drunken lunch at which Emlyn had baited Wilder about contemporary fiction for hours, hostile in some way Wilder couldn't place, never once naming what he already knew.

And before that lunch, the scene in the hotel abroad: Emlyn asking about a letter held for her at the desk, addressed in a hand he recognized; Odile confessing; Emlyn saying only that he had always been fonder of his friend than of his wife. She had gone back afterward to the rented rooms and said nothing whatever about the trip, and the afternoon had passed exactly as the others had, Wilder unknowing, the secret folded inside the secret.

Further back still lay the ordinary machinery of the affair — the rented rooms in the quiet district, filled with linen and plates as though domesticity itself could be borrowed for a few afternoons a week; Odile's announcement that she was carrying her husband's child, and their mutual decision that the rooms would go on exactly as before, unaltered by that fact. And furthest back of all, at the very beginning, the party at Emlyn's house, the crowd drinking downstairs while Wilder led Odile up into a room alone and told her how lovely she was, crossing, in that quiet upstairs air, from admiration into betrayal.

Now, at the end of all of it, sitting opposite Emlyn in the evening light, Wilder understood that the story he had been telling himself — of secrecy kept, then broken, then confessed — had never been the true order of things. Emlyn had known before the lunch, before the dinners, before the rooms were even closed. He had carried the knowledge through every game of racquets discussed, every glass raised, every silence held at his own table. Wilder felt something give way in him that was not quite shame and not quite relief. Emlyn only refilled his glass, unhurried, and said that he supposed they had both been rather bad at knowing what they had, and worse at saying so, and that it hardly mattered now which of them had lied longer.

Listen: he says he has been unstuck in time so many times that he no longer tries to tell it in order, and neither will I.

He is on the radio, telling the city that every moment always exists, that free will is a notion peculiar to Earth, that he has seen the fourth dimension from the inside of a zoo enclosure on another world, sharing the glass with a film actress who liked him better than she let on. The host is polite. The switchboard fills with people who think he is either a prophet or a symptom.

His daughter, hearing the broadcast played back to her by a neighbor, decides her father has gone soft in the head, and within the month she has his checkbook and his keys and the running of his house, and believes, honestly, that she is saving him.

He is a boy in an industrial town, small and strange, the kind of child other children test rather than befriend. His father takes him to a pool one afternoon to make a swimmer of him, throws him into the deep end, and the boy sinks, and finds, on the tiled bottom, that he does not especially want to come back up. He will remember the bottom of that pool for the rest of his life, the way you remember a room you were happy in.

He is married to the daughter of the man who owns the optometry school, and for some years this is simply what his life is: a practice, a good address, money that arrived without much explanation, the ordinary comfort of being someone's husband. Then there is a plane in the mountains, and he walks out of the wreckage more or less intact, and his wife, driving frantic to reach the hospital where they've taken him, dies quietly of carbon monoxide leaking into the car, so that his survival and her death arrive as the same news.

Before any of that — or after it, it hardly matters how you hold the deck — he is a soldier, if you can call it that, a chaplain's assistant with no training worth the name, lost behind the lines with a scout who beats him when he says he would rather be left to die where he is. They are captured. The scout's leg goes bad on the prison train and he dies blaming the boy with his final breath, and somewhere in the boxcars this blame becomes a promise: a fellow prisoner tells him, calmly, that he will be killed one day on the dead scout's account, whenever that day comes.

He is housed with enemy officers who have, through some clerk's error, been drawing double rations for years and look embarrassingly well for prisoners of war. He is moved on to a great city and put underground with other captives in a disused abattoir, in the cold room meant for carcasses. One night the sky opens with fire and by morning the city above them is gone, simply gone, and they climb up into ash where streets used to be. They are made to dig the dead from sealed cellars until one of the diggers, a young man, dies of nothing but the horror of it, the dry heaves taking him the way illness takes other men.

He comes home and collapses and is hospitalized, and another patient hands him paperback novels by a hack writer of interplanetary romances, and something in these cheap books fits the shape of what he cannot otherwise say.

He is on another planet, in a zoo, and his keepers explain patiently that time is not a river but a mountain range, that every moment is already standing there to be visited, that his species' devotion to cause and effect is a kind of provincialism.

He is on a stage years later, addressing a crowd, telling them the exact hour of his death, which he has always known, and a man he cannot place lifts something that is not quite a gun, and the light that comes out of it finishes what a dying scout started on a train whose year no one troubles to remember.

His daughter, hearing the broadcast played back to her by a neighbor, decides her father has gone soft in the head, and within the month she has his checkbook and his keys and the running of his house, and believes, honestly, that she is saving him.

He is a boy in an industrial town, small and strange, the kind of child other children test rather than befriend. His father takes him to a pool one afternoon to make a swimmer of him, throws him into the deep end, and the boy sinks, and finds, on the tiled bottom, that he does not especially want to come back up. He will remember the bottom of that pool for the rest of his life, the way you remember a room you were happy in.

He is married to the daughter of the man who owns the optometry school, and for some years this is simply what his life is: a practice, a good address, money that arrived without much explanation, the ordinary comfort of being someone's husband. Then there is a plane in the mountains, and he walks out of the wreckage more or less intact, and his wife, driving frantic to reach the hospital where they've taken him, dies quietly of carbon monoxide leaking into the car, so that his survival and her death arrive as the same news.

Before any of that — or after it, it hardly matters how you hold the deck — he is a soldier, if you can call it that, a chaplain's assistant with no training worth the name, lost behind the lines with a scout who beats him when he says he would rather be left to die where he is. They are captured. The scout's leg goes bad on the prison train and he dies blaming the boy with his final breath, and somewhere in the boxcars this blame becomes a promise: a fellow prisoner tells him, calmly, that he will be killed one day on the dead scout's account, whenever that day comes.

He is housed with enemy officers who have, through some clerk's error, been drawing double rations for years and look embarrassingly well for prisoners of war. He is moved on to a great city and put underground with other captives in a disused abattoir, in the cold room meant for carcasses. One night the sky opens with fire and by morning the city above them is gone, simply gone, and they climb up into ash where streets used to be. They are made to dig the dead from sealed cellars until one of the diggers, a young man, dies of nothing but the horror of it, the dry heaves taking him the way illness takes other men.

He comes home and collapses and is hospitalized, and another patient hands him paperback novels by a hack writer of interplanetary romances, and something in these cheap books fits the shape of what he cannot otherwise say.

He is on another planet, in a zoo, and his keepers explain patiently that time is not a river but a mountain range, that every moment is already standing there to be visited, that his species' devotion to cause and effect is a kind of provincialism.

He is on a stage years later, addressing a crowd, telling them the exact hour of his death, which he has always known, and a man he cannot place lifts something that is not quite a gun, and the light that comes out of it finishes what a dying scout started on a train whose year no one troubles to remember.
